659.title: Sukkot: guests from the past
659.hook: each night mystical guests are welcomed: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and in many homes Sarah and others
659.howItsDone: On each night of Sukkot many families recite an invitation to the ushpizin in the sukkah, and many add women guests (ushpizot); hosting real guests and giving to the poor is considered part of the custom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first nail after the fast. Your line was from fasting to building. What next thing did you start? Today, the sukkah is finished, and someone's at the door. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

The first night of Sukkot. The hut is up: three walls of canvas or plywood, a roof of branches with stars showing through, paper chains made by children, a string of lights. The family squeezes in around a folding table. And before the meal, in many homes, someone reads an invitation. Not to the neighbors. To Abraham. Please come in, take your seat. And they mean it, in their way. Tonight Abraham leads the guests.
screen: `STARS THROUGH THE BRANCHES.` → `AN INVITATION BEFORE THE MEAL.` → `TONIGHT, ABRAHAM.`

segments.voice: The custom comes from the Zohar, the great book of Jewish mysticism. It calls these visitors ushpizin, an Aramaic word for guests. Seven of them, one leading each night of the festival: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph and David. All seven come every night, the mystics say, but each night a different one is the main guest. Why these seven? Many of them were wanderers. Abraham left home for a land he didn't know. Jacob fled. Joseph was carried off to Egypt. Moses led a people through the desert in huts. David hid in caves. They know what it's like to live in a temporary shelter. In many homes today, women are welcomed too, ushpizot: Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Leah, Miriam, Abigail, Esther, or other lists, depending on the community. The Zohar doesn't stop at the invitation. It says the guests' portion belongs to the poor. If you invite Abraham and set a lovely table but no one hungry eats from it, the guests get up and leave. Abraham, after all, was famous for running out of his tent to welcome strangers. So the mystical guests and the real ones are linked. You honor the heroes of the past by feeding someone in the present. Some families leave an empty chair. Others hang the names on the sukkah wall. Many make sure an actual guest is at the table every night.
screen: `USHPIZIN: GUESTS, IN ARAMAIC.` · `SEVEN WANDERERS, ONE A NIGHT.` · `USHPIZOT: THE WOMEN TOO.` · `THEIR PORTION GOES TO THE POOR.` · then, large: `INVITE THE GUESTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite someone to eat. Picture your table, wherever it is. Now picture one person from the past you'd want at it: a grandparent, a teacher, a figure from the stories. Welcome them in your mind. Then ask: who, alive and nearby, might need a seat at that table this week? Someone new in town, someone alone, someone struggling. If you pray, you can ask for an open door. If not, just decide who you'll invite. The bell holds the time.
Ushpizin. Guests. The seven figures from the past welcomed into the sukkah, one leading each night, whose portion goes to the poor.
Your line: invite the guests. Today, send one real invitation to share a meal or a coffee with someone who might be alone. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

660.title: Sukkot: Ecclesiastes
660.hook: Ecclesiastes, with its hard truths about time, is read in the season of joy
660.tomorrow: Sukkot: the season of our joy (Deuteronomy 16:14–15)
660.howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi synagogues the book of Ecclesiastes (Kohelet) is read on the Shabbat during Sukkot, or on Shemini Atzeret when no Shabbat falls in the intermediate days; Sephardi communities generally do not read it publicly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ushpizin, guests from the past. Your line was invite the guests. Did a real invitation go out? Today, a guest of a different kind: a book that sits down at the festival table and says something uncomfortable. Day six hundred sixty.

It's the happiest festival of the Jewish year. The harvest is in. The sukkah is decorated. People are eating outside under the branches. And on the Shabbat of Sukkot, in many synagogues, the reader stands up and chants a book that opens like this: "Vanity of vanities, saith Koheleth; vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Everything is fleeting. Nothing lasts. What's the point of all your work? It's like inviting the gloomiest uncle to the party. On purpose.
screen: `THE HAPPIEST FESTIVAL.` → `VANITY OF VANITIES.` → `THE GLOOMY UNCLE, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The book is Ecclesiastes. In Hebrew, Kohelet, the name its speaker gives himself. It probably means one who gathers, or one who speaks to a gathering, from kahal, an assembly. Tradition identifies him with King Solomon. And the word translated vanity, hevel, literally means a breath, a vapor. Not worthless, exactly. Fleeting. Like breath on a cold morning: there, then gone. Kohelet looks hard at life. The rich die like the poor. The wise die like fools. You work, and someone else inherits it. There's nothing new under the sun. And then he says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." A time to be born, a time to die, a time to weep, a time to laugh. Why read this at Sukkot? Several reasons are given. One is that Sukkot is the harvest festival, when people feel richest and most secure, and Kohelet is a reminder not to mistake the barns for forever. Another: the sukkah itself teaches the same lesson. You leave your solid house to sit in a hut that a wind could knock over. And Kohelet doesn't end in despair. Again and again he comes back to joy: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart." Enjoy life with the people you love, he says, all the fleeting days. That's the paradox. Joy isn't the opposite of knowing things pass. It may be the right response to it. The festival gets a guest who keeps its eyes open. Sephardi communities generally don't read the book publicly; many Ashkenazi ones do.
screen: `KOHELET: THE ONE WHO GATHERS.` · `HEVEL: BREATH, VAPOR.` · `A TIME TO EVERY PURPOSE.` · `EAT THY BREAD WITH JOY.` · then, large: `JOY WITH OPEN EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line of Ecclesiastes. Take this one: a time to weep, and a time to laugh. Say it slowly, twice. Then think of something good in your life right now that won't last forever: a child's age, a friendship in its easy season, the light this time of year. Hold it, knowing it's fleeting, and let yourself enjoy it anyway, maybe more because of that. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Kohelet. Ecclesiastes. The book of breath and fleeting things, read in the season of joy, which still tells you to eat your bread with joy.
Your line: joy with open eyes. Today, enjoy one ordinary pleasure fully, knowing it will pass. Day six hundred sixty.

661.title: Sukkot: the season of our joy (Deuteronomy 16:14–15)
661.hook: the festival the Torah commands joy for most
661.howItsDone: During the seven days of Sukkot, Jews eat meals in the sukkah, wave the four species, and in the festival prayers call the holiday zman simchateinu, the season of our joy; many hold Simchat Beit HaShoevah celebrations with music and dancing at night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet, the book of breath. Your line was joy with open eyes. Which fleeting pleasure did you enjoy? Today, the Torah turns joy into a commandment. Day six hundred sixty-one.

Can you be commanded to be happy? It sounds absurd. Feelings don't take orders. If someone told you, be joyful, starting now, you'd probably feel worse. And yet that's what the Torah does, more for this festival than any other. In the prayers, each festival gets a nickname. Passover is the season of our freedom. Shavuot is the season of the giving of the Torah. And Sukkot, the week in the flimsy hut, is called zman simchateinu. The season of our joy.
screen: `CAN JOY BE COMMANDED?` → `FREEDOM, TORAH, AND...` → `THE SEASON OF OUR JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse in Deuteronomy: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy man-servant, and thy maid-servant, and the Levite, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, that are within thy gates." And the next verse ends: "and thou shalt be altogether joyful." A midrash counts: the Torah mentions joy three times for Sukkot, once for Shavuot, and not at all for Passover. Why the most here? One reason given is the harvest. At Passover the grain is still in the field; who knows what will happen? At Sukkot, it's gathered in. You can finally exhale. Now look at who's on the list. Not just you and your family. Your workers. The Levite, who owned no land. The stranger. The orphan. The widow. The joy the Torah commands isn't a mood. It's a guest list. Maimonides makes this sharp in his law code. Someone who eats and drinks with his family and locks the gate, and doesn't feed the poor and the bitter of heart, isn't rejoicing in a mitzvah. That's only the joy of his stomach. And in the days of the Temple, Sukkot nights had the water-drawing celebration, with torches, music and dancing until dawn. The Mishnah says: whoever didn't see that rejoicing never saw joy in their life. So can joy be commanded? Maybe not the feeling. But the conditions can be: a table, a harvest, the door open to people who wouldn't otherwise be there. And joy has a way of showing up where it's been made welcome.
screen: `THOU SHALT REJOICE IN THY FEAST.` · `THREE TIMES FOR SUKKOT.` · `JOY IS A GUEST LIST.` · `THE WATER-DRAWING, TILL DAWN.` · then, large: `SEASON OF OUR JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one joy today. Sit, and look for it on purpose. Not a big one. A warm drink, a song you love, a text from a friend, the light on a wall. Name it. Stay with it a while. Then do the Torah's second step: think who's not at your table. Someone lonely, someone grieving, someone new. How could a little of your joy reach them? If you pray, you can thank God for the joy. The bell holds the time.
Sukkot. Booths. The harvest festival called the season of our joy, when the Torah commands rejoicing, with the stranger, orphan and widow at the table.
Your line: season of our joy. Today, share one joy with someone who wouldn't otherwise have it. Day six hundred sixty-one.

662.title: Hoshana Rabbah
662.hook: the seventh day: seven circuits, and willows beaten on the ground
662.tomorrow: Shemini Atzeret: stay one more day
662.howItsDone: On Hoshana Rabbah, many synagogues make seven circuits with the lulav and etrog while chanting the hoshanot, then each person strikes a small bundle of willow branches on the ground; some communities also keep a night of study beforehand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukkot, the festival the Torah commands joy for most. Your line was season of our joy. Did you find one joy, and did you stop long enough to feel it? Today, the last day of the week in the booth. Day six hundred sixty-two.

It's early morning in a synagogue on the seventh day of Sukkot. Every day this week, people have walked once around the reading table holding the palm branch and citrus, chanting. Today they go around seven times. The room is crowded, the line is slow, and somebody's lulav keeps poking the person in front. Then, when the circling is done, people pick up small bundles of willow twigs, a few branches tied together, and strike them on the floor. Leaves fly. Kids love this part. Adults, if they're honest, do too. The day has a name that sounds like a shout.
screen: `THE SEVENTH DAY OF SUKKOT.` → `SEVEN TIMES AROUND.` → `WILLOWS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Hoshana Rabbah means the great hoshana. Hoshana is a plea: save, please. It comes from the Psalm sung on festivals, in the old Jewish translation: "We beseech Thee, O LORD, save now!" All week, after each circuit, people chant short prayers called hoshanot, each one asking for rescue, for rain, for the harvest. On the seventh day, the circuits and the pleas pile up to seven, and the day earns the word great. Then the willows. The Mishnah, in tractate Sukkah, describes willow branches set up around the altar in the Temple, and the people circling it. After the Temple fell, the willow stayed. The Talmud calls beating the willow a custom of the prophets: not a commandment from the Torah, but very old and kept with care. Why willows? The rabbis noticed that the willow has no fruit and no smell. In one well-known midrash, it stands for people with neither learning nor good deeds. And the willow grows by water, so on a festival where people begin to ask for winter rain, it fits. A later layer came from the mystics. In the Zohar's tradition, Hoshana Rabbah is the very end of the season of judgment that began on Rosh Hashanah, the moment the sealed verdict is finally sent out. So some people stay up the night before, reading Deuteronomy and Psalms, and greet each other with a wish for a good note. Striking the willows, in that reading, is a way of knocking something loose: the last of the year's heaviness, shaken off and left on the floor.
screen: `HOSHANA: SAVE, PLEASE.` · `SEVEN CIRCUITS, SEVEN PLEAS.` · `A CUSTOM OF THE PROPHETS.` · `THE LAST DOOR OF JUDGMENT.` · then, large: `BEAT THE WILLOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: shake off one heaviness. Sit or stand, and breathe out slowly. Name one thing you've been carrying since the fall began: a worry, a grudge, a mistake you keep replaying. Hold it in mind, the way you'd hold a bundle of twigs. Now, if you like, tap your hands on your knees, or on the table, five times. Let each tap loosen it a little. Then let your hands rest open, and breathe for whatever time is left. The bell holds the time.
Hoshana Rabbah. The great save-us. Seven circuits, a bundle of willows, and the year's last judgment let go. Today's word.
Your line: beat the willows. Today, when that heaviness comes back, tap twice on whatever's near you and leave it there. Day six hundred sixty-two.

663.title: Shemini Atzeret: stay one more day
663.hook: Rashi: like a king who asks his children to stay one more day
663.howItsDone: Shemini Atzeret is a full festival day after Sukkot, kept with festive meals and synagogue services; the prayer for rain (Tefillat Geshem) is chanted, and the mention of rain enters the daily Amidah from that day until Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hoshana Rabbah, seven circuits and a bundle of willows. Your line was beat the willows. Did you leave one heaviness on the floor? Today, the day after the festival ends, that isn't quite over. Day six hundred sixty-three.

Everyone knows the end of a family visit. The bags are by the door. The car is packed. Somebody has already said, we should really get going. And then a grandmother, or an aunt, or a parent who doesn't say this kind of thing out loud, says: stay. Just one more night. There's nothing planned. No outing, no big meal. They just aren't ready for the house to be empty yet. The Torah's festival calendar has a day exactly like that, right at the end of Sukkot. It has almost no rituals of its own. And the most famous explanation of it is a story about a family that doesn't want to say goodbye.
screen: `THE BAGS ARE BY THE DOOR.` → `STAY. JUST ONE MORE NIGHT.` → `A DAY WITH ALMOST NO RITUALS.`

segments.voice: Shemini Atzeret means the eighth day of assembly. In the old Jewish translation of Leviticus, after seven days of Sukkot, "on the eighth day shall be a holy convocation unto you," and then: "it is a day of solemn assembly." That's the word atzeret. Its root has to do with holding back, stopping, staying. Here is the strange part. The eighth day has no sukkah requirement, no lulav, no willows. In the Land of Israel, people step out of the booth and back into the house. So what is the day for? Rashi, the great eleventh-century commentator, answers with a parable, drawn from the midrash. A king invites his children to a feast for a set number of days. When the time comes for them to leave, he says: your parting is hard for me. Please, stay one more day. That's the whole holiday. A week of crowds, guests, palm branches and booths, and then one quiet day that's only about being together. The Talmud adds another layer. Over the seven days of Sukkot, the Temple offered seventy bulls, and the rabbis connected those seventy to the seventy nations of the world. On the eighth day, a single bull: a small, private meal after the big banquet. Today, Shemini Atzeret has one notable addition. In the standing prayer, people begin to mention rain, and many synagogues chant a special prayer for it. Winter is coming in the Land of Israel. The asking begins on the day when nobody is in a hurry to leave.
screen: `THE EIGHTH DAY OF ASSEMBLY.` · `NO BOOTH, NO LULAV, NO WILLOWS.` · `A KING SAYS: STAY ONE MORE DAY.` · `SEVENTY BULLS, THEN ONE.` · then, large: `STAY ONE MORE DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: linger with someone you love. Before the bell, bring one person to mind, near or far. Picture the last time you said goodbye to them, and how quickly it went. Now, for this sit, imagine you didn't leave. You stayed. No plan, no agenda, just the two of you in the same room. Breathe with that. If you can, sometime today, add five unhurried minutes to a call or a visit. The bell holds the time.
Shemini Atzeret. The eighth day of assembly, the day God, in Rashi's parable, asks the children to stay. Today's word.
Your line: stay one more day. Today, when you're about to rush off from someone, stay a few minutes longer than you planned. Day six hundred sixty-three.

664.title: Simchat Torah: seven circles
664.hook: seven dancing circuits with the Torah scrolls
664.howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, communities take every Torah scroll from the ark and dance seven hakafot around the reading table, then read the end of Deuteronomy and the start of Genesis; many call all the children up together under a large tallit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemini Atzeret, the eighth day of assembly. Your line was stay one more day. Did you stay a little longer with someone? Today, the party that ends the season. Day six hundred sixty-four.

Picture a synagogue where nobody is sitting down. The ark is open and empty, because every scroll is out, in somebody's arms. A man in his eighties holds one, then hands it to a teenager. Children run between legs waving flags. Someone starts a song, the circle tightens, and the whole crowd goes around the reading table, singing, sometimes spilling out the door and into the street. Then the music stops, the scrolls change hands, and it starts again. And again. By the end of the night, people have gone around seven times, and almost nobody has kept count.
screen: `THE ARK IS EMPTY.` → `EVERY SCROLL IN SOMEONE'S ARMS.` → `AROUND AND AROUND.`

segments.voice: Simchat Torah means rejoicing of the Torah. In the Land of Israel it falls on Shemini Atzeret itself; outside Israel, where the festival has an extra day, it comes the day after. Either way, it marks one thing: the yearly reading of the Torah is finished, and immediately begun again. The last words of Deuteronomy are read, about the great things Moses did, in the old Jewish translation, "in the sight of all Israel." Then, without a pause, Genesis: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The person honored with the ending is called the bridegroom of the Torah. The one honored with the beginning is called the bridegroom of Genesis. Today, in many communities, women are honored this way too. The dancing circuits are called hakafot, from a Hebrew root meaning to go around. You've met circuits already this week: on Sukkot, with the lulav, one a day, and seven on Hoshana Rabbah. Now the circling continues, but with the scroll instead of the palm branch, and with dancing instead of pleas. The Bible says nothing about this day. The name Simchat Torah comes centuries after the Talmud, and the custom of seven dancing hakafot is later still, spreading widely in the early modern period. It grew from the people up, not from a verse down. In many synagogues, every child is called to the Torah together under one large prayer shawl, held up over them like a roof. And everyone, scholar or not, gets a turn to hold the scroll and dance.
screen: `THE LAST WORD, THEN THE FIRST.` · `BRIDEGROOMS OF THE TORAH.` · `HAKAFOT: GOING AROUND.` · `A CUSTOM FROM THE PEOPLE UP.` · then, large: `DANCE WITH THE SCROLL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: dance once today. It doesn't have to be good. Before the bell, think of a book, a song, a teaching you love enough to carry around. Picture holding it in your arms. Breathe with that for a moment. Then, if you're somewhere you can, stand up and turn around once, slowly, a small circle. Or sway where you sit. Let your body do what your heart does when something you love comes back around. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Hakafot. Circuits, goings-around: seven dancing circles with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah. Today's word.
Your line: dance with the scroll. Today, go back to the first page of something you love, a book, an album, a teaching, and begin it again. Day six hundred sixty-four.

665.title: Hanukkah: the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 4)
665.hook: the revolt against Antiochus and the Temple rededicated, told in the books of Maccabees
665.howItsDone: Hanukkah is kept for eight nights from the twenty-fifth of Kislev, with candles lit each night and the Al HaNissim prayer added to the daily prayers and grace after meals, recalling the Hasmonean victory and the rededication.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hakafot, the seven circles of Simchat Torah. Your line was dance with the scroll. Did you start something you love over again? Today the calendar jumps ahead two months, into winter. Day six hundred sixty-five.

A small band of fighters walks up to the Temple in Jerusalem, and stops. The gates are burned. The priests' rooms are torn down. Weeds have grown up in the courtyards, the text says, like a forest or a hillside. The altar has been used for offerings their law forbids. These are men who have just won battles against a much larger army. And the first thing they do, standing in the ruin, is tear their clothes and put ashes on their heads, the way you'd mourn a death. The story of Hanukkah, in its oldest telling, starts with grief.
screen: `THE GATES ARE BURNED.` → `WEEDS LIKE A FOREST.` → `A STORY THAT STARTS WITH GRIEF.`

segments.voice: The oldest account is the First Book of Maccabees, written within a few generations of the events. It isn't in the Jewish Bible; it was preserved in Greek, and it's part of the Catholic and Orthodox Christian Bibles. Here's the story it tells. In the 160s before the common era, the Greek king Antiochus the Fourth ruled the land. He banned Torah study, circumcision and Shabbat, and set up a pagan altar in the Temple. Some Jews went along; others resisted. In the village of Modiin, an old priest named Mattathias refused to offer a pagan sacrifice, and fled to the hills with his five sons. One son, Judah, nicknamed the Maccabee, led a guerrilla army. Before one battle, as the book tells it, his men were afraid of the size of the enemy. Judah answered that victory doesn't depend on numbers; strength comes from heaven. Chapter four is the homecoming. They pull down the defiled altar, and here's a detail people love: they don't know what to do with its stones. So they store them on the Temple mount, the text says, until a prophet should come and tell them. Then they build a new altar of whole stones, light the lampstand, and on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev, they dedicate it, with songs and harps and cymbals, for eight days. Judah decrees the days be kept every year. Hanukkah means dedication. Later, the prayer added on Hanukkah thanks God for delivering the many into the hands of the few.
screen: `A BOOK OUTSIDE THE JEWISH BIBLE.` · `ANTIOCHUS BANS THE TORAH.` · `JUDAH: STRENGTH COMES FROM HEAVEN.` · `A NEW ALTAR, EIGHT DAYS.` · then, large: `THE FEW AGAINST THE MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand for one thing you value. Sit tall, and breathe. Name one thing you care about that feels outnumbered in your life right now: honesty at work, rest in a busy house, a practice nobody around you shares. Hold it the way the Maccabees held those altar stones, carefully, without rushing to decide everything. Then choose one small way to stand for it today. Breathe with that choice. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. Dedication: the altar rebuilt and the Temple rededicated, for eight days, in the month of Kislev. Today's word.

Your line: the few against the many. A week of guests in the booth, joy with open eyes, the season of our joy, beaten willows, one more day, the dance, and now the few. Today, do your one small thing, even if you're the only one. Day six hundred sixty-five.
